title: Adrenal tumour imaging: clinical, molecular, and radiomics perspectives
abstract: Adrenal tumours have become a common incidental finding in the radiological evaluation of patients. Estimates suggest that 1-10% of the general population currently harbours an adrenal tumour, peaking in prevalence in the seventh and eighth decades of life. Advances in CT and MR have contributed to improved characterisation of adrenal masses, and novel radiopharmaceuticals are being developed for molecular characterisation and disease subtyping. As a result, the imaging and management of adrenal tumours have been important subjects of many guidelines and consensus statements. New radiomics approaches, together with machine learning, are now being introduced and are quickly shaping the way that imaging data are analysed and interpreted. Furthermore, the development of theranostics links the molecular biology of functioning tumours to targeted treatment options. In this Review, we summarise up-to-date imaging and follow-up approaches for adrenal tumours to provide patients with the most accurate diagnosis, thereby avoiding unnecessary additional tests or surgery.

title: A quarter-century of progress: innovations in lipid medicine that transformed cardiovascular prevention
abstract: This TimeCapsule reviews the major transformations in lipid metabolism and cardiovascular disease prevention during the first quarter of the 21st century and their impact on clinical practice. From late 20 th century paradigms to current state-of-the-art strategies, the field has consolidated statins as foundational therapy while establishing the clinical benefit of non-statin agents and introducing biological therapies into cardiovascular disease prevention. These developments support the paradigm that lowering LDL-cholesterol levels earlier and sustaining this over time translates to greater reductions in cardiovascular risk. More recently, RNA-targeted and DNA-targeted approaches have enabled the modulation of proteins, such as PCSK9, lipoprotein(a), apolipoprotein C-III, and ANGPTL3. The traditional concept of HDL-cholesterol being considered a good cholesterol has been challenged, whereas the causal relevance of lipoprotein(a) has gained recognition. New metrics-including non-HDL-cholesterol, apolipoprotein B, triglyceride-rich remnants, or remnant cholesterol-are increasingly integrated into residual risk assessment. A growing sex-specific perspective has refined cardiovascular research and care. Despite robust evidence, the proportion of patients meeting their recommended targets remains unacceptably low. Implementation science seeks to address this persistent evidence-practice gap. In parallel, artificial intelligence is reshaping scientific methodologies and is poised to transform the understanding and management of lipid-related cardiometabolic disease.

title: Clinical and metabolic subtypes of recent-onset adult type 1 diabetes: a prospective cohort study
abstract: BACKGROUND: Adult-onset type 1 diabetes exhibits substantial heterogeneity. We aimed to investigate whether this variability reflects distinct disease entities or different temporal stages of a shared autoimmune process. METHODS: In this prospective cohort study, we analysed data from adults (aged 18-69 years) in the German Diabetes Study who had clinically diagnosed type 1 diabetes within the preceding 12 months, and from individuals who were positive for glutamic acid decarboxylase antibody (GADA) but had originally been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. We used unsupervised machine learning based on GADA status, fasting C-peptide, glucose, triglycerides, and HDL cholesterol to characterise clinical and metabolic type 1 diabetes subtypes. The resulting subtypes were compared for aetiological traits (polygenic risk scores for type 1 diabetes and type 2 diabetes, partitioned type 2 diabetes polygenic risk scores, human leukocyte antigen [HLA] profiles, and islet-directed autoantibodies), insulin sensitivity, glucagon-stimulated C-peptide trajectories as a measure of residual β-cell function, and complications during prospective follow-up. Reproducibility was assessed in adults with type 1 diabetes from the German Diabetes Prospective Follow-up Registry (Diabetes-Patienten-Verlaufsdokumentation [DPV]). FINDINGS: Analysed participants in the German Diabetes Study cohort were recruited between June 27, 2005, and Jan 20, 2025 (n=600), and were followed up for a mean of 6·1 (SD 4·7) years. We identified three type 1 diabetes subtypes: two GADA-positive subtypes, and one GADA-negative subtype. A similar clinical and metabolic subtype structure was observed in the DPV cohort, whose participants were recruited between 2000 and 2025 (n=483) and were followed up for a mean of 3·1 (SD 5·0) years. One GADA-positive subtype was characterised by lower BMI, higher insulin sensitivity, and severe β-cell dysfunction (classic type 1 diabetes), whereas the second showed higher BMI, lower insulin sensitivity, and better β-cell function (mixed type 1 diabetes). The two GADA-positive subtypes did not differ in autoimmunity or type 1 diabetes polygenic risk scores, whereas the GADA-negative subtype had lower genetic type 1 diabetes risk, despite no clear subtype-specific differences in HLA risk haplotypes. Longitudinal modelling indicated that the mixed type 1 diabetes group was positioned 6·1 years (95% CI 4·6-7·8) earlier along the β-cell function decline trajectory compared with the classic type 1 diabetes group. The risks of hypoglycaemia (log-rank p=0·0019), retinopathy (mixed type 1 diabetes vs classic type 1 diabetes: adjusted hazard ratio 4·93 [95% CI 1·71-14·24]), and cardiovascular autonomic neuropathy (log-rank p=0·028) differed across the groups. INTERPRETATION: Our results indicate that individuals with combined autoimmunity and lower insulin sensitivity present with clinical diabetes earlier than classic type 1 diabetes along the β-cell decline trajectory, identifying a potential timeframe for disease-modifying interventions in specific type 1 diabetes subtypes.
